extra_misconceptions.fact: Board games rely on a central shared playing surface for spatial movement, while card games use shuffled decks as the primary medium.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Card games and board games belong to the exact same game medium because both are played on a tabletop.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Abstract games like chess or Tetris operate strictly through formal rules, geometry, and objectives without needing a narrative theme.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Every game must include a detailed fictional story and setting in order to have a playable theme.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Game resources include any quantifiable asset players manage to reach objectives, including time, health points, turns, and hand cards.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Resources in a game only refer to physical tokens like play money, wooden cubes, or plastic miniatures.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Play value comes from the psychological and social rewards a player experiences, such as strategic challenge, socialization, or novelty.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Play value is determined strictly by how expensive a game's graphics or physical components are to produce.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a game's core objectives and rules if you strip away its narrative theme completely?
Which structural distinction separates a cooperative player format from a team-versus-team competition?
What specific columns in your four-game comparison chart reveal how different mediums manage scarce resources?
Under what condition does a physical outdoor game require boundary markers and safety rules before play begins?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Complexity measures the burden of rules a player must track, whereas depth measures the meaningful strategic choices emerging from them.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Complexity and depth mean the exact same thing when evaluating a game's rulebook and decision space.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Asymmetric games achieve balance when different starting powers and abilities still give equally skilled players a fair chance to win.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A balanced game gives every player the exact same starting pieces, abilities, and board position.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Board and card games also rely on interface design through clear iconography, readable card layouts, and intuitive player reference boards.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Interface design only applies to digital menus and heads-up displays inside computer or console video games.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Heavy reliance on random chance reduces the impact of strategic planning and shifts outcomes toward luck rather than player skill.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Adding pure dice rolls to every combat resolution increases the strategic skill required to win a match.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to strategic depth when a game adds dozens of complex rules that offer only one winning path?
Which gameplay indicator shows that a multiplayer game suffers from poor balance rather than high difficulty?
Where should a designer place critical status information in an interface design so players react in real time?
Why is it important to check ESRB or age-appropriateness ratings before introducing a video game to younger Scouts?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Copyright protects only the specific written expression of the rulebook and original artwork, not the underlying game mechanics or rules.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Copyright law protects the core rules and dice-rolling mechanics of a tabletop game from being used by others.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Trademarks protect brand names, logos, and slogans that identify the commercial source, while copyright protects original creative works.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Trademarks and copyrights are interchangeable legal terms for protecting a video game's source code and music.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Using copyrighted assets requires explicit licensing permission from the rights holder, even if you give full attribution and charge nothing.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Giving credit to the original creator in the credits allows you to use copyrighted music or art in your own game.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Publishing a game based on an existing franchise requires negotiating a formal licensing agreement with the intellectual property owner.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Buying a retail copy of a Star Wars novel grants you the legal right to publish a Star Wars board game.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to the underlying game mechanics of a board game when its artwork and rulebook text are copyrighted?
Which legal protection prevents a competing studio from using a confusingly similar brand logo on its game box?
What documentation confirms that a game studio holds legal permission to build a game around a licensed movie property?
Why is it dangerous for an indie developer to publish a fan game using copyrighted characters without a license?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Changing multiple rules at once confounds the playtest results, making it impossible to isolate which specific rule caused an issue.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Testing five new house rules simultaneously is the fastest way to see how each individual rule changes a game.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Altering objective point values shifts player incentives immediately, often causing players to abandon old strategies for new exploits.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Modifying a single victory point value only changes the final score and never alters how players make decisions.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Recording your hypothesis before playing is essential so you can honestly compare expected player behavior against actual playtest data.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Predictions about a rule change can be written down after the playtest match finishes so they match the outcome.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Completing a full baseline game under standard rules is necessary to understand how mid-game and endgame mechanics normally interact.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Playing one partial round under the standard rules is enough to establish a baseline before changing the rules.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to your ability to tell which rule change caused a bug if you modify three rules at the same time?
Which written prediction must you record in your notebook before testing a modified rule in a live match?
What observable player behavior during a modified match confirms whether your rule change sped up or slowed down pace?
Why is it dangerous to alter boundary or physical contact rules in a sport like kickball without checking field safety?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A game design notebook is a working chronological log that captures initial vision statements, rough sketches, rule drafts, and revisions.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A game design notebook is a polished marketing brochure created only after the final game is completely finished.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Scouts must secure counselor approval of the written game concept in Requirement 5 before starting prototype construction in Requirement 6.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: You should build all final artwork and game components before asking your counselor to review your game concept.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A vision statement is a concise high-level summary that captures the core experience, medium, player format, theme, and main objective.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A vision statement is a step-by-step turn sequence that lists every edge case and scoring tiebreaker in the game.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Preliminary rules serve only as a starting playable hypothesis that will be revised repeatedly once real playtesting reveals flaws.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Preliminary rule lists must be permanently locked in before any physical prototype pieces are cut out or tested.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a game project during development when the designer lacks a clear vision statement in their notebook?
Which section of your preliminary rules defines the exact actions a player takes from the start of a turn to its end?
What specific milestone must you record in your design notebook before you build the physical or digital prototype?
Under what condition does an outdoor or physical game concept require equipment and play-area safety specifications?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Early prototypes should use cheap materials like index cards, pencil, and spare tokens so you can rewrite or discard parts without hesitation.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: An initial game prototype needs professional graphic design, laminated cards, and 3D-printed pieces to be testable.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Loopholes and dominant strategies are flaws in the rule system itself that the designer must fix by adjusting costs, limits, or incentives.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: When a playtester finds an overpowered loophole, you should blame the player for not playing in the spirit of the game.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Requirement 6 requires completing at least three separate cycles of playtesting, analyzing flaws, revising the rules, and testing again.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Running a single playtest session with three different friends satisfies the iterative testing requirement.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A dead end occurs when the rules trap a player or the game state in a position where no legal moves or progress toward victory can be made.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A game dead end only happens when a player loses all their health points and gets eliminated from the match.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a competitive match when a player discovers a degenerate loophole that guarantees an easy victory?
Which physical materials allow you to build an early tabletop prototype that can be edited in seconds between tests?
What details must you log in your notebook across each of your three mandatory playtest and revision cycles?
Why is it dangerous to skip inspecting prototype equipment and playing surfaces before testing a physical game?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Blind playtesting means new players set up and play the game using only the written instruction sheet, with zero help from the designer.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Blind playtesting means the test players wear blindfolds or test the game without knowing its title or theme.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Coaching players or answering questions masks gaps in the rulebook that real buyers would face when opening the game at home alone.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Answering one quick setup question from a confused player during a blind test keeps the test accurate and on track.

extra_misconceptions.fact: When uncoached testers misinterpret a rule, the instruction sheet is unclear, poorly organized, or missing a visual setup diagram.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: If blind testers misread a rule and play a phase wrong, the testers simply failed to pay close enough attention.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Blind testing requires a fresh group of players who have never played the game before so prior memory does not fill in missing rules.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Blind playtesting can be performed using the same group of friends who helped you test your earlier prototypes.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to the validity of a blind playtest if you step in to explain a confusing rule while the group is playing?
Which essential sections must appear on your written instruction sheet so uncoached players can finish a full game?
Where should you direct your attention and note-taking while a group reads your rule sheet during a blind playtest?
Under what condition is a designer allowed to interrupt a live blind playtest before the players finish the session?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Professional game designers spend their days writing detailed specifications, balancing spreadsheets, scripting levels, and analyzing playtests.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Game designers spend most of their workday playing finished video games and coming up with cool story ideas.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Modern game studios rely on specialized roles including producers, sound designers, writers, quality assurance testers, and user researchers.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: You must be an expert 3D animator and C++ engine programmer to work in any role inside the game industry.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Requirement 8 explicitly requires obtaining both parent or guardian permission and counselor approval before meeting with an industry pro.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A Scout can message any game developer online for an interview without getting parent or counselor permission first.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Game studios evaluate applicants heavily on a portfolio of completed prototypes, mods, and team projects alongside formal coursework.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Earning a college degree in game design guarantees a studio job even if you have never built a playable project.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a commercial game project if programmers, artists, and audio engineers work without a producer's schedule?
Which core responsibilities distinguish a systems or level designer from a software engineer on a development team?
What interview questions help you document how an educator's curriculum prepares students for studio team roles?
Which two approvals and Youth Protection rules must be in place before you schedule a game industry interview?
